hook.text: The Sydney Opera House was budgeted for four years. It took fourteen. Every planner thought this time was different.

buildup.text: Kahneman found people predict project times by best-case scenarios and ignore base rates of delay.

discovery.text: The planning fallacy: we underestimate time, cost, and risk while overestimating our own efficiency.

twist.text: Even knowing about this bias barely helps. People who learn it still underestimate their own plans.

climax.text: The fix: use reference class forecasting. Ask how long similar projects took, not how long yours feels.

punchline.text: Your plan is not special. Check the base rate.

quiz.question: What is the planning fallacy?
options: Overestimating costs to seem cautious
Underestimating time and cost based on best-case thinking
Refusing to plan ahead at all

hook.text: Traders with more data made worse predictions than those with less. More information felt like more skill.

buildup.text: Paul Slovic gave horse bettors 5 facts, then 40. Their accuracy stayed flat but confidence doubled.

discovery.text: Extra information increases confidence faster than it increases accuracy. The gap is the illusion.

twist.text: Experts are most vulnerable. Specialists drown in data and mistake familiarity for understanding.

climax.text: Before deciding, ask: does this new data change my prediction or just my confidence? Test honestly.

punchline.text: More data is not more wisdom. Know the difference.

quiz.question: What happened when bettors received more data in Slovic's study?
options: Accuracy and confidence both rose
Confidence rose but accuracy stayed flat
Both accuracy and confidence dropped

hook.text: After the 2008 crash, everyone claimed they saw it coming. Before the crash, almost nobody acted on it.

buildup.text: Hindsight bias rewrites memory. Once you know the outcome, your brain inserts it into the past as obvious.

discovery.text: Fischhoff proved this in 1975: people given outcomes rated them as predictable even when they were random.

twist.text: This bias blocks learning. If every outcome feels obvious, you never update how you make decisions.

climax.text: Record your predictions before events happen. Comparing forecasts to outcomes reveals your real accuracy.

punchline.text: If you knew it all along, prove it. Show the receipt.

quiz.question: Why does hindsight bias block learning?
options: It makes failures seem too painful to revisit
It makes outcomes feel obvious so you never improve your process
It erases all memory of the event

hook.text: Doctors told patients surgery had a 90% success rate. Actual success was 50%. Their confidence outran reality.

buildup.text: Calibration means your confidence matches your accuracy. Say 80% sure and be right 80% of the time.

discovery.text: Most people are overconfident. They say 90% sure but are right only 70% of the time. The gap is measurable.

twist.text: Weather forecasters are well-calibrated because they get daily feedback. Most professionals never do.

climax.text: Track your confident predictions. After fifty, check the hit rate. Reality is the only calibration tool.

punchline.text: Confidence without calibration is just guessing loudly.

quiz.question: Why are weather forecasters well-calibrated?
options: They use supercomputers
They receive fast, daily feedback on predictions
They are naturally less biased than others

hook.text: A bank robber covered his face with lemon juice, sure cameras could not see him. He was genuinely shocked.

buildup.text: Dunning and Kruger tested people on logic and grammar. The worst performers rated themselves near the top.

discovery.text: Low skill prevents you from recognizing low skill. You need competence to even judge competence.

twist.text: High performers underestimate themselves. They assume their ease means the task is easy for everyone.

climax.text: To escape the trap, seek expert feedback early. You cannot self-assess in domains where you lack skill.

punchline.text: The less you know, the less you know you don't know.

quiz.question: What did Dunning and Kruger find about low performers?
options: They rated themselves accurately
They rated themselves near the top despite poor results
They refused to participate in the study

hook.text: An investor loved a stock and only read bullish articles. He ignored five warnings that predicted the crash.

buildup.text: Confirmation bias makes us seek evidence that supports what we already believe and skip the rest.

discovery.text: Wason's card test showed people verify rules instead of trying to disprove them. We test to confirm.

twist.text: Social media amplifies this. Algorithms feed you content you agree with, creating invisible echo chambers.

climax.text: Force yourself to seek one strong counterargument before every decision. Disconfirmation is a discipline.

punchline.text: The evidence you avoid is the evidence you need.

quiz.question: What does Wason's card test reveal?
options: People naturally seek to disprove rules
People seek to confirm rules rather than disprove them
People ignore all evidence equally

hook.text: In World War II, the military reinforced planes where bullet holes clustered. Abraham Wald said they were wrong.

buildup.text: The holes showed where planes survived damage. The missing holes showed where planes did not come back.

discovery.text: Survivorship bias: we study winners and ignore the dead. The visible sample misleads because losers vanish.

twist.text: Startup advice suffers from this. We study unicorns and copy their habits, ignoring millions that did the same.

climax.text: Always ask: where are the ones that did not survive? The absent evidence is often the most important.

punchline.text: You can't learn from winners if you ignore the losers.

quiz.question: What did Wald realize about the bullet holes on returning planes?
options: The holes showed where to add armor
The holes showed where planes could survive hits, not where they needed armor
The holes were randomly distributed

hook.text: A cab hit someone at night. A witness said it was blue. The city has 85% green cabs. Was it really blue?

buildup.text: Most people say blue because the witness seems reliable. They forget that green cabs outnumber blue ones 5 to 1.

discovery.text: Base rate neglect: we overweight vivid evidence and underweight boring background statistics.

twist.text: Even trained doctors fall for it. A positive test with 5% false positive rate in a rare disease is usually wrong.

climax.text: Before trusting vivid evidence, check the base rate first. Frequency matters more than your gut feeling.

punchline.text: The boring statistic usually beats the dramatic story.

quiz.question: What is base rate neglect?
options: Ignoring all statistical evidence
Overweighting vivid evidence while ignoring background frequency
Always trusting the base rate over witnesses

hook.text: Steve Jobs dropped out and took a calligraphy class. People call it visionary. It was a lucky accident.

buildup.text: We turn random sequences into neat causal stories. Nassim Taleb calls this the narrative fallacy.

discovery.text: Stories compress chaos into logic. They feel satisfying but hide the randomness that actually drives events.

twist.text: History books are narrative fallacies at scale. They present luck and chaos as intention and strategy.

climax.text: When a story sounds too clean, add noise back in. Ask: what role did luck and timing actually play here?

punchline.text: A great story is not the same as a true explanation.

quiz.question: What is the narrative fallacy?
options: Ignoring all stories and relying only on data
Turning random events into neat causal stories that hide chaos
Believing that narratives are always more accurate than statistics

hook.text: One shark attack makes national news. Suddenly everyone thinks sharks are a top killer.

buildup.text: An availability cascade starts with a dramatic event. Media covers it, people discuss it, media covers it more.

discovery.text: Repetition creates perceived truth. A risk mentioned often enough feels common even when data says it is rare.

twist.text: Policy follows. Billions are spent on terrorism prevention while heart disease, a far bigger killer, is underfunded.

climax.text: When a risk feels huge, check the actual numbers. Dramatic does not mean frequent. Media distorts probability.

punchline.text: What you hear most is rarely what kills most.

quiz.question: What drives an availability cascade?
options: Careful statistical analysis by experts
Media repetition making rare events feel common
Government campaigns to raise awareness

hook.text: You sit through a terrible movie because you paid for the ticket. The money is gone either way.

buildup.text: Sunk costs are past expenses that cannot be recovered. Rationally, they should not affect future choices.

discovery.text: But we feel that quitting wastes the investment. So we invest more to justify what we already lost.

twist.text: The Concorde jet continued for decades despite losses. Governments kept funding to avoid admitting the sunk cost.

climax.text: Ask: if I had not already invested, would I start this now? If no, the sunk cost is trapping you. Walk away.

punchline.text: The money is gone. The only question is what to do next.

quiz.question: What is the sunk cost trap?
options: Avoiding all investments to prevent loss
Continuing a losing course because of past investment that can't be recovered
Accurately calculating total investment before deciding

hook.text: A company spent $50 million on a failing project. Instead of stopping, they approved another $30 million.

buildup.text: Escalation of commitment means increasing investment in a failing course of action to justify prior decisions.

discovery.text: Staw's research showed that decision-makers who felt responsible for the initial choice escalated the most.

twist.text: Bringing in a new decision-maker reduces escalation. Fresh eyes have no ego invested in the past choice.

climax.text: Set kill criteria before starting any project. Predetermined exit points remove ego from the stop decision.

punchline.text: Choose your exit point before the stakes rise.

quiz.question: What reduces escalation of commitment according to research?
options: Giving the original decision-maker more authority
Bringing in a new decision-maker with no ego in the past choice
Increasing the budget to show confidence

hook.text: A CEO publicly declared a strategy brilliant. Six months later, data proved it wrong. She doubled down anyway.

buildup.text: Once we commit publicly, changing course feels like admitting failure. Consistency becomes a cage.

discovery.text: Cialdini showed that public commitments create internal pressure to stay consistent, even against new evidence.

twist.text: Wise leaders reframe changing direction as learning, not failure. Flexibility is strength, not weakness.

climax.text: When defending a past position, ask: am I protecting the idea or my ego? The answer changes everything.

punchline.text: Foolish consistency is the mind's most expensive lock.

quiz.question: Why is public commitment a trap?
options: Others will enforce the commitment legally
It creates internal pressure to stay consistent even against new evidence
Public commitments always lead to better outcomes

hook.text: Students given free mugs demanded $7 to sell them. Students without mugs would only pay $3. Same mug, double the price.

buildup.text: Thaler's endowment effect: owning something makes it feel more valuable. Possession distorts valuation.

discovery.text: This is loss aversion applied to ownership. Losing what you have feels worse than gaining something equal.

twist.text: Investors hold losing stocks because selling feels like a loss. The endowment effect traps capital in bad bets.

climax.text: Ask: would I buy this thing today at this price? If not, you are overvaluing it just because you own it.

punchline.text: Owning it does not make it worth more.

quiz.question: What does the endowment effect cause?
options: People undervalue things they own
People overvalue things simply because they own them
People trade freely without emotional attachment

hook.text: Most organ donation rates depend on the default option on a form, not on how people feel about donation.

buildup.text: Status quo bias is the preference for keeping things as they are. Change requires effort; staying put is free.

discovery.text: Samuelson and Zeckhauser showed people stick with defaults even when alternatives are clearly better.

twist.text: Companies exploit this with auto-renewals. The default keeps customers paying even when they want to leave.

climax.text: Review your defaults annually: subscriptions, investments, routines. Ask if you would choose them today from scratch.

punchline.text: The default is a decision someone else made for you.

quiz.question: What drives high organ donation rates in some countries?
options: Strong cultural beliefs about donation
The default option on the form is opt-in
People feel strongly about saving lives

hook.text: A car dealer lists a car at $30,000. After haggling to $25,000, you feel you won. The car was worth $22,000.

buildup.text: Anchoring means the first number you hear sets a reference point. All later judgments drift toward it.

discovery.text: Tversky and Kahneman spun a rigged wheel. High numbers made people guess higher answers to unrelated questions.

twist.text: Even experts fall for anchors. Judges given random numbers before sentencing gave harsher or lighter sentences.

climax.text: When you see a first number, pause. Generate your own estimate independently before comparing. Break the anchor.

punchline.text: The first number wins unless you set your own.

quiz.question: How does anchoring affect decisions?
options: It makes people ignore all numbers entirely
The first number heard sets a reference that biases later judgments
It only affects novice decision-makers

hook.text: A $200 shirt seems expensive. Place it beside a $2,000 suit and suddenly it feels like a bargain.

buildup.text: The contrast effect: our perception of something changes depending on what we compare it to. Context shifts value.

discovery.text: Real estate agents show a terrible house first. The next house looks amazing by contrast, even if it is average.

twist.text: Salary negotiations use this. A high first offer makes a moderate counter-offer feel like a concession.

climax.text: Judge every option on its own merits, not relative to what came before. Comparisons are chosen to manipulate you.

punchline.text: What something sits next to changes what it looks like.

quiz.question: Why do real estate agents show a bad house first?
options: To test if buyers are paying attention
To make the next house look better by contrast
Because bad houses are easier to sell

hook.text: A magazine offered digital for $59 and print-plus-digital for $125. Few chose print. Then they added print-only at $125.

buildup.text: The print-only option was a decoy. Nobody chose it, but it made print-plus-digital look like a steal.

discovery.text: The decoy effect: adding an inferior option makes a target option look more attractive by comparison.

twist.text: Movie theatres use this with popcorn. The medium is priced near the large to push you toward the large.

climax.text: When three options appear and one seems pointless, it is there to nudge you. Spot the decoy and decide without it.

punchline.text: The worst option on the menu is there on purpose.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a decoy option?
options: To give customers a genuine low-cost alternative
To make a target option look better by comparison
To reduce the total number of choices

hook.text: You drive 20 minutes to save $10 on a $30 item. You skip the same $10 discount on a $500 item. The $10 is identical.

buildup.text: Relative thinking makes us evaluate savings as percentages, not absolutes. $10 off $30 feels big.

discovery.text: Thaler showed this with mental accounting. We treat money differently depending on its context, not its value.

twist.text: This is why luxury stores offer small expensive add-ons. A $50 case for a $1,000 phone feels like nothing.

climax.text: Evaluate money in absolute terms. Ten dollars is ten dollars no matter the context.

punchline.text: A dollar saved is a dollar saved. Percentages lie.

quiz.question: What is relative thinking in behavioral economics?
options: Always considering inflation in financial decisions
Evaluating savings as percentages rather than absolute amounts
Comparing prices across different stores systematically

hook.text: Two TVs side by side: the $2,000 model looks clearly better. At home, alone on the wall, they look identical.

buildup.text: Distinction bias: differences seem larger when options are compared side by side than when experienced separately.

discovery.text: Hsee found people overpay for tiny upgrades that are visible in comparison mode but invisible in experience mode.

twist.text: Marketers arrange products to maximize visible differences. In isolation, most mid-range products feel identical.

climax.text: Before paying for an upgrade, imagine using each option alone. If the difference vanishes, skip the premium.

punchline.text: You buy in comparison mode. You live in experience mode.

quiz.question: What does distinction bias cause?
options: People ignore all differences between products
Small differences seem larger in comparison mode than in actual use
People always choose the cheapest option

hook.text: People who liked nuclear power said it was low-risk and high-benefit. Those who disliked it said the opposite.

buildup.text: The affect heuristic: feelings substitute for analysis. If something feels good, we judge it as safe and beneficial.

discovery.text: Slovic showed emotions act as a shortcut. Instead of calculating risk, we ask: how do I feel about this?

twist.text: This is why dread risks like terrorism feel huge while common risks like car crashes feel minor. Emotion overrules math.

climax.text: When a decision triggers strong feelings, pause. Separate your emotional reaction from the actual evidence. Then choose.

punchline.text: Your feelings about the risk are not the risk itself.

quiz.question: What is the affect heuristic?
options: Using data to override emotional reactions
Using feelings as a shortcut for risk and benefit judgments
Deliberately ignoring emotions in all decisions

hook.text: When full, you swear you will eat healthy tomorrow. When hungry, you grab the pizza. You can't predict your hungry self.

buildup.text: Loewenstein's empathy gap: in a cold emotional state, we cannot imagine how we will act in a hot emotional state.

discovery.text: This explains broken diets, angry emails, and impulsive purchases. Calm you and emotional you're different.

twist.text: The gap works both ways. In a hot state, you cannot imagine ever feeling calm about this issue again. But you will.

climax.text: Make important decisions in a cold state. Set rules while calm that bind you when emotions run hot.

punchline.text: Never trust the promises of your calm self to your future angry self.

quiz.question: What is the hot-cold empathy gap?
options: Unable to predict behavior in a different emotional state
Always making decisions in a heated state
Feeling empathy only when emotionally calm

hook.text: Shoppers who grocery-shop while hungry buy 64% more junk food. They project current hunger onto future meals.

buildup.text: Projection bias means assuming your future preferences will match your current ones.

discovery.text: Loewenstein showed people overestimate how long current feelings will last. Happiness fades; misery fades.

twist.text: Gym memberships spike in January when motivation is high. By March, the mood fades but the contract remains.

climax.text: Before a big decision, ask: will I still feel this way in six months? If unsure, delay or add a cancellation option.

punchline.text: Today's feeling is a terrible forecast of tomorrow.

quiz.question: What is projection bias?
options: Projecting your feelings onto other people
Assuming future preferences will match current ones
Planning for the worst-case scenario

hook.text: You keep a losing stock because selling would make the loss real. As long as you hold, regret stays hypothetical.

buildup.text: Regret aversion means avoiding action to dodge the pain of a bad outcome. Inaction feels safer than a wrong choice.

discovery.text: Zeelenberg found people regret actions more than inactions in the short term, but reverse this over a lifetime.

twist.text: Old people regret things they did not do far more than mistakes they made. Inaction feels safe now but stings later.

climax.text: Ask: will I regret not doing this in ten years? Long-term regret comes from inaction, not from trying and failing.

punchline.text: The safest choice now is often the most regretted later.

quiz.question: What do people regret most over a lifetime?
options: Actions that failed
Things they never tried
Decisions made too quickly

hook.text: Lottery winners and accident survivors return to baseline happiness within a year.

buildup.text: Impact bias: we overestimate how long and how intensely future events will affect our emotional state.

discovery.text: Gilbert and Wilson call it affective forecasting failure. We imagine future joy or pain as permanent.

twist.text: This bias fuels bad trades. We chase promotions expecting lasting happiness and dread failures expecting lasting pain.

climax.text: Before making a fear-based or desire-based decision, remember: you'll adapt. The feeling will be shorter than you think.

punchline.text: Nothing feels as long as you think it will.

quiz.question: What does impact bias cause us to do?
options: Accurately predict future emotional states
Overestimate how long future events will affect our feelings
Ignore future emotions entirely

hook.text: JFK's advisors unanimously backed the Bay of Pigs invasion. Everyone agreed and nobody questioned. It was a disaster.

buildup.text: Janis coined groupthink: cohesive groups suppress dissent to maintain harmony. Unanimity replaces critical thinking.

discovery.text: Warning signs: an illusion of invulnerability, pressure on dissenters, self-censorship, and shared stereotyping.

twist.text: After Bay of Pigs, JFK restructured meetings. He assigned a devil's advocate and left the room to reduce conformity.

climax.text: In important group decisions, appoint someone to argue against the consensus. Dissent is a feature, not a bug.

punchline.text: When everyone agrees too fast, nobody is thinking.

quiz.question: What did JFK do after the Bay of Pigs to prevent groupthink?
options: Fired all his advisors
Assigned a devil's advocate and left the room during discussions
Stopped holding group meetings entirely

hook.text: In 1999, everyone bought internet stocks because everyone else was buying. By 2001, the market had lost $5 trillion.

buildup.text: Herd behavior: we follow the crowd because we assume others know something we do not. It feels safe to follow.

discovery.text: Information cascades form: early movers act, followers copy, and the chain grows even when nobody has good information.

twist.text: The herd can be right sometimes. But when it is wrong, everyone crashes together. Diversified thinking beats crowds.

climax.text: Before following the crowd, ask: do I've independent evidence or am I just copying? The distinction matters enormously.

punchline.text: A crowd is not a reason. It is just a crowd.

quiz.question: What drives an information cascade?
options: Everyone independently analyzing the same data
Early movers act and followers copy without independent evidence
Government regulation of market behavior

hook.text: Milgram's subjects shocked strangers to dangerous levels because a man in a lab coat told them to continue.

buildup.text: Authority bias: we defer to perceived experts even when their instructions conflict with our own judgment and ethics.

discovery.text: The uniform, title, or credential triggers automatic obedience. We stop evaluating and start complying.

twist.text: Con artists exploit this with fake titles and suits. The appearance of authority is often enough to bypass skepticism.

climax.text: When someone claims authority, verify their credentials and check if their expertise matches the decision at hand.

punchline.text: A title is not an argument. Demand the evidence.

quiz.question: What triggers authority bias?
options: Careful evaluation of an expert's evidence
Perceived credentials like titles, uniforms, or confidence
Personal experience with the authority figure

hook.text: A restaurant with a long queue draws more customers. An empty restaurant repels them. Same food, different perception.

buildup.text: Social proof: when uncertain, we look at what others are doing and copy it. Crowds signal quality to our brain.

discovery.text: Cialdini showed hotel towel reuse jumped 33% when signs said most previous guests reused. Peer behavior is powerful.

twist.text: Fake reviews exploit this. Over 30% of online reviews are fabricated, yet they heavily influence purchase decisions.

climax.text: When social proof drives your choice, verify independently. Popularity is evidence of popularity, not quality.

punchline.text: Everyone doing it does not mean it is right.

quiz.question: What did Cialdini's hotel towel experiment show?
options: Signs about environmental impact worked best
Telling guests that most previous guests reused towels was most effective
Offering discounts increased towel reuse the most

hook.text: Smoke fills a room. Nobody leaves because nobody else is leaving. Everyone privately panics but publicly stays calm.

buildup.text: Pluralistic ignorance: everyone privately rejects a norm but assumes everyone else accepts it.

discovery.text: Latane and Darley's bystander experiments showed that more witnesses paradoxically reduce the chance anyone helps.

twist.text: In meetings, everyone stays silent on a bad idea, each thinking they are the only one who sees the flaw. Nobody speaks.

climax.text: Break the spell by going first. One dissenting voice frees others to speak. Silence is the trap, not agreement.

punchline.text: If everyone seems fine with it, maybe nobody truly is.

quiz.question: What is pluralistic ignorance?
options: Everyone genuinely agreeing with a group decision
Everyone privately disagreeing but assuming everyone else agrees
Ignoring information from multiple sources
